strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art single-step audio generation with 100x speedup (RTF 0.013), demonstrating significant practical value for deployment
Comprehensive evaluation including multiple objective metrics, human subjective evaluation with 10 professionals, and extensive ablation studies validating each component
Well-designed training methodology: instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow mix-up effectively addresses training instability and is convincingly validated through ablations
Clever integration of classifier-free guidance into training objective, eliminating runtime overhead while maintaining controllable generation
Compact model (120M parameters) trainable on consumer GPUs (~70 hours on 4 RTX 3090s), with efficient latent space modeling
Clear presentation with precise algorithms, informative architecture diagrams, and detailed experimental setup enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: Mean Flows formulation from concurrent Geng et al. (2025), Flux-style architecture adapts existing designs (Esser et al. 2024), dual encoder is straightforward combination; primary novel contribution is the curriculum strategy which is incremental

Experimental comparison concerns: Table 1 mixes re-evaluated open-source with transcribed paper results creating inconsistency; comparisons use different training datasets; 100x speedup claim compares 1 NFE vs. 200 NFEs without per-NFE efficiency analysis

Training curriculum ablation (Table 3) confounds effects: FluxAudio trained on full dataset while MeanAudio-Scratch trained only on AudioCaps, making it difficult to isolate curriculum contribution from dataset effects
Heavy dependence on pre-trained components (FLAN-T5, CLAP, VAE, vocoder) and two-stage initialization from FluxAudio makes it difficult to isolate what is methodologically novel

Substantial acknowledged limitations: restricted to 10-second audio segments, cannot generate speech or handle fine-grained linguistic content, trained on 98% weakly-labeled data from LLMs/MLLMs with no analysis of label quality impact
Multi-step generation only competitive not superior: at 25 steps achieves FD=13.38 but TangoFlux achieves FD=20.65 at 50 steps; advantage primarily in efficiency not quality

Insufficient analysis of results: no error cases discussed, missing qualitative examples in main paper, limited investigation of why 75% flow mix-up ratio is optimal, Table 8 dual-encoder evaluation uses only 3 annotators on 10 samples

Theoretical justification gaps: Equation 3 (integrated CFG) lacks optimality justification and sensitivity analysis; Section 3.5 explanation of mean flow training failure is empirical not rigorous; Mean Flow Identity connection to single-step quality not intuitive

Evaluation concerns: metrics based on PANNs may not capture perceptual or linguistic fidelity; CLAP score has known limitations; human evaluation limited to 10 samples per configuration without inter-annotator agreement reporting

Code unavailable during review (only promised); complex two-stage pipeline makes exact reproduction difficult; relationship to concurrent flow-based approaches (FlashAudio, AudioTurbo) not deeply discussed

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving SOTA single-step generation with 100x RTF speedup over diffusion baselines on multiple metrics (FAD, FD, KL, IS, CLAP)
Well-motivated instantaneous-to-mean curriculum with flow field mix-up that is thoroughly validated through ablation studies showing necessity of each component
Clever integration of classifier-free guidance into training targets to eliminate inference overhead without compromising quality
Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple datasets (884k samples) and thorough ablations (Tables 2-4) demonstrating training stability
Practical advantages: lightweight 120M parameter model trainable on consumer GPUs in 3 days, self-contained without requiring teacher models
Clear technical presentation with sound mathematical formulation and well-structured algorithmic descriptions
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation details and promised open-sourcing of code and weights
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: applies MeanFlow from concurrent work (Geng et al. 2025) in relatively straightforward manner; main novel contributions (curriculum, CFG integration) are incremental engineering contributions

Evaluation fairness concerns: models compared with different training data amounts/sources, different text encoders, and inconsistent CFG integration status (Table 1 footnotes); marginal speedup over ConsistencyTTA (0.013 vs 0.017 RTF) undermines '100x' claim
Lack of human evaluation: relies solely on automated metrics without listening tests or qualitative audio comparisons; no validation that generated audio is perceptually better

CFG integration insufficiently analyzed: claim that training-time guidance achieves equivalent inference-time guidance lacks theoretical justification or empirical validation; effective scale formula assumes equivalence without proof

Training curriculum requires manual dataset quality designation and hyperparameter tuning (75% flow mix-up ratio); instability at 0% and 25% ratios (Table 3) suggests fragility; limited guidance for domain transfer
Architectural contributions not ablated: heavy borrowing from Flux (MMDiT, DiT blocks, ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm) without isolating their contributions from MeanFlow itself
Abstract inconsistency (RTF stated as 0.013 vs 0.016 in text); multi-step generation claims ('smooth and coherent transitions') unvalidated; limited failure case analysis

Questionable design choices lack justification: hyperparameters (ω=0.3, κ=0.9, logit-normal μ=0.4/σ=1), batch size difference between stages, hidden dimension 448, block counts N1=4/N2=8 appear arbitrary
